reason: There are over 10 cross-referenced claims regarding the 1967 discovery, the Vela satellites, and the subsequent scientific breakthroughs.
story: In 1967, the U.S. launched Vela satellites to catch the Soviet Union hiding nuclear tests in space. On July 2, sensors detected a flash of gamma radiation, but it didn't match a nuclear bomb's signature. It wasn't a secret weapon; it was the brightest explosion in the universe. This discovery was so sensitive it stayed classified for six years. In 1973, researchers revealed 'Gamma-Ray Bursts'—brief, catastrophic events from deep space. These bursts release more energy in seconds than our Sun will in its entire 10-billion-year life. They occur when massive stars collapse or neutron stars collide, beaming radiation across billions of light-years. We now detect roughly one every day. These 'cosmic beacons' are so powerful they can be seen across the observable universe, all discovered because we were looking for Cold War secrets.
angle: The most powerful explosions in the universe were discovered by accident by Cold War satellites hunting for secret Soviet nuclear tests.

claims.claim: The discovery was made by the U.S. military's Vela satellites.
The satellites were specifically looking for secret nuclear weapon tests in space.
The discovery remained classified or unreleased until 1973.
Ray Klebesadel led the team at Los Alamos that published the first paper on the discovery.
Gamma-ray bursts are distributed randomly across the sky rather than concentrated in the Milky Way.
A single gamma-ray burst can release more energy in seconds than the Sun will in 10 billion years.
Long-duration bursts (over two seconds) are caused by the collapse of massive stars.
Short-duration bursts (under two seconds) are caused by the merger of neutron stars.
The first 'afterglow' of a burst was detected in February 1997.
Satellites now detect roughly one gamma-ray burst per day.
The energy of these bursts is concentrated into narrow, focused jets.
NASA's Swift satellite was launched in November 2004 to study these events.
The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope was launched in June 2008 to observe bursts.
The burst GRB 970508 was the first to have its distance measured at roughly 6 billion light years.
The burst GRB 190114C reached extreme energy levels of 1 Tera electron volt (TeV).

disputed: S1 mentions a hypothesized third class of GRBs involving white dwarf mergers, but S4 only identifies two primary categories; attribute as 'according to one theory'.
Scientific consensus on the existence of radio afterglows was disputed until the 1997 discovery of GRB 970508, as noted in S1.
